notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether hand can be partitioned into groups of groupSize consecutive values.
Idea: Count card values and repeatedly start groups at the smallest remaining value.
Technique and why it applies: The minimum remaining card must begin a group, because no smaller value remains to pair with it. Each required consecutive value is decremented, and exhausted minima are removed from the heap.
Invariant: freq records remaining copies of each value, and min_heap contains values with positive counts.
Edge cases: collections and heapq are not imported in the snippet. groupSize must be positive; zero would cause modulo-by-zero. The algorithm assumes a valid frequency count for each exhausted heap minimum.
Complexity: Heap operations and group formation take roughly O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether a hand can be divided into consecutive groups of size W.
Idea: Count occurrences and repeatedly remove the smallest remaining card, requiring W consecutive values.
Technique and why it applies: A smallest remaining value must start the next group. The code decreases counts for each value in the sequence and returns False if any count becomes negative.
Invariant: counts stores remaining multiplicities; the heap supplies candidate starting values in ascending order.
Edge cases: The heap is built from the entire hand, so duplicate entries remain and zero-count values are skipped when they reach the top. W must be positive and divide hand length.
Complexity: Heapify is O(n), and the repeated pops and group scans give O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest walk that visits every node of a connected graph at least once.
Idea: Compute all-pairs shortest distances, then use memoized recursion over the current node and a bitmask of unvisited nodes.
Technique and why it applies: Each transition chooses a node still in mask and pays its shortest-path distance from x. The recursion removes that node from the mask and minimizes total distance.
Invariant: fn(x,mask) is the minimum additional distance needed to visit all nodes represented by mask from x.
Edge cases: inf and cache are used without imports in the snippet. The recursion's state semantics should be checked: paying shortest-path distances between selected nodes does not explicitly update the visited mask for intermediate nodes traversed on those shortest paths, so it may overcount or fail to model a walk correctly.
Complexity: Floyd–Warshall takes O(n³); memoized mask recursion has O(n·2^n) states and up to O(n) transitions per state.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of edges in a walk that visits every graph node.
Idea: Run multi-source BFS from every node, with the visited state consisting of both current node and a bitmask of visited vertices.
Technique and why it applies: Each edge traversal adds one step and updates the bitmask. BFS explores these states in increasing path length, and the first distance among full-mask states is minimal.
Invariant: dp[mask][node] is the shortest distance to reach node having visited exactly the vertices represented by mask.
Edge cases: The code relies on the graph being connected, as guaranteed by the problem; otherwise min(dp[-1]) can remain infinity. It enqueues each state only when first discovered.
Complexity: There are O(n·2^n) states and O(E·2^n) transitions, so time and space are O(E·2^n) and O(n·2^n), respectively.

Task and constraints: Apply each shift to the prefix of s ending at the corresponding index, wrapping lowercase letters around the alphabet.
Idea: Compute suffix sums of shifts modulo 26, then shift each character by its accumulated amount.
Technique and why it applies: A character at index i receives all shifts from i through the end. Reducing the cumulative sum modulo 26 avoids repeated full alphabet wraps.
Invariant: nums[i] is the total shift affecting s[i], modulo 26.
Edge cases: The code repeatedly subtracts 26 until the code point is in range, rather than using modulo at character conversion. It assumes lowercase letters and equal lengths for s and shifts.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for nums and the output string.

Task and constraints: Shift each lowercase character by the sum of all shifts from its position to the end.
Idea: Initialize the suffix sum of shifts modulo 26, emit each shifted character, then subtract the current shift before advancing.
Technique and why it applies: The running times value is exactly the sum of shifts still affecting the current character. Modulo 26 handles wraparound.
Invariant: times is the total shift for the current index, modulo 26.
Edge cases: Empty strings return an empty result. The method assumes shifts has one entry per character.
Complexity: One pass uses O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Choose an empty seat maximizing the distance to the nearest occupied seat.
Idea: Find occupied seat indices, evaluate both ends, and compute half the length of every internal gap.
Technique and why it applies: At an internal gap between occupied seats x and y, the best seat is near the midpoint and has distance floor((y-x)/2). At either edge, the distance is the number of empty seats before the first or after the last occupied seat.
Invariant: seat_nums contains the occupied indices in sorted order, and each candidate in the max expression represents a best distance for one gap or edge.
Edge cases: If no seat is occupied, min(seat_nums) and max(seat_nums) fail; the problem guarantees at least one occupied seat. Empty internal gaps contribute no entries.
Complexity: Collecting indices and evaluating gaps take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the empty seat with the greatest distance to the closest occupied seat.
Idea: Scan seats while remembering the previous occupied position and update the best distance for leading, internal, and trailing gaps.
Technique and why it applies: The leading distance is the first occupied index; internal gaps use half the separation; the trailing distance is the count after the final occupied seat.
Invariant: prev is the latest occupied seat index and result is the best candidate distance found so far.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees at least one occupied seat. result starts at one, which is harmless for valid inputs but not a general initialization for all possible seat arrays.
Complexity: A single scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the total area covered by the union of axis-aligned rectangles, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sweep horizontal y-events while a segment tree tracks the total covered x-length.
Technique and why it applies: Between event y-coordinates, the covered x-length is constant, so area increases by vertical distance times cur_x_sum. Segment-tree cover counts track intervals with at least one active rectangle.
Invariant: cur_x_sum is the union length of active x-intervals at the current sweep line.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used but not imported. The segment-tree update uses inclusive compressed indices and accesses xs[tr+1]; the root range is initialized to len(xs)-1, so the implementation should be checked for an out-of-range endpoint at the right edge.
Complexity: Sorting 2R events costs O(R log R); each update is O(log R) segment-tree work, with O(R) compressed-coordinate space.

Task and constraints: Find the union area of a set of rectangles using a vertical sweep and segment tree.
Idea: Sort opening and closing events by y, maintaining the covered x-length as events are processed.
Technique and why it applies: The area between consecutive y values equals the vertical gap times the current covered x-length. The segment tree's count tracks full coverage, and total stores the covered length of each interval.
Invariant: cur_x_sum is the total active x-length after the previous event.
Edge cases: The code assumes rectangles is nonempty because it reads events[0]. X must contain at least two distinct coordinates. Event ordering at equal y values is consistent with the sorted tuple order, with closing events (-1) before opening events (1).
Complexity: Event sorting is O(R log R), and each segment-tree update is O(log R) over O(R) compressed coordinates; space is O(R log R) in the dynamic tree worst case.

Task and constraints: For each person, find the quietest person who is at least as rich as them.
Idea: Process the richer-than relation in topological order and propagate the quietest known person along each directed edge.
Technique and why it applies: Edges go from richer person a to poorer person b. When a is processed, arr[a] is the quietest person known among a and richer ancestors, so b can update its candidate.
Invariant: arr[v] stores the index of the quietest person among v and all richer people processed upstream.
Edge cases: collections is used without importing it. The relation is assumed acyclic, as guaranteed by the problem; otherwise nodes in cycles may never enter the queue.
Complexity: Topological processing takes O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Find the peak index in a mountain array that strictly increases and then strictly decreases.
Idea: Binary-search the slope, moving right while the sequence is increasing and left when it is decreasing.
Technique and why it applies: The peak is where the comparison between arr[mid] and arr[mid+1] changes from increasing to decreasing. beg converges to that index.
Invariant: The peak remains within the current search interval.
Edge cases: The code accesses arr[mid+1] without checking bounds; the mountain-array guarantee and chosen mid positions are relied on to avoid indexing past the end. The array must have a valid interior peak.
Complexity: Binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Return the index of the maximum element in a mountain array.
Idea: Binary-search for the transition from increasing to decreasing.
Technique and why it applies: If arr[mid] is greater than its next value, the peak lies at mid or to the left; otherwise it lies to the right. The loop narrows the interval to the peak index.
Invariant: left is the first possible index of the peak, while right is the last possible candidate.
Edge cases: The code reads arr[mid+1] even when mid could be the last index, but the strict mountain constraints normally keep the search from testing that position. Input length is at least three.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count car fleets that reach target, where faster cars behind slower cars join them.
Idea: Sort cars by starting position from nearest to target backward and compare their arrival times.
Technique and why it applies: A car forms a new fleet only if it arrives later than the fleet ahead; otherwise it catches up and joins that fleet.
Invariant: arrival_bound is the arrival time of the slowest fleet encountered nearest the target so far.
Edge cases: The condition not arrival_bound treats zero as uninitialized, but valid cars before target have positive arrival times. Equal arrival times join one fleet.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), the scan is O(n), and the paired list uses O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of swaps needed to transform s1 into s2 when the strings are anagrams.
Idea: Fix positions from left to right, swapping the first mismatched character with a later character that matches the needed target character.
Technique and why it applies: Once positions before i match, only the suffix remains. A matching swap places the required character at i and the recursion advances.
Invariant: Every recursive call has a matching prefix before i, and dp[i][curr] memoizes the remaining swap cost for that suffix state.
Edge cases: sys is used without import. The memo key includes the entire current string, but the code may recurse into a state with no matching character if inputs are not anagrams; the problem guarantees anagrams.
Complexity: The search can branch exponentially in n; memo space depends on the number of distinct (i,string) states.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps to make A equal B, where each swap exchanges two characters in A.
Idea: Use BFS over strings, generating neighbors by swapping the first mismatched position with a later character matching B at that position.
Technique and why it applies: Fixing the earliest mismatch avoids wasting swaps on already-correct prefixes. Each edge is one swap, so BFS finds the shortest sequence.
Invariant: Every state at BFS depth result can be reached in result swaps, and lookup prevents duplicate states from being enqueued.
Edge cases: neighbors assumes there is a mismatched position; it is called only after s==B is checked. The inputs must be anagrams so a matching character exists later.
Complexity: The number of states can be factorial in string length; each state may generate O(n) neighbors, with exponential/factorial time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string, where () has score one and concatenation adds scores while nesting doubles them.
Idea: Track nesting depth and add a power of two whenever a closing parenthesis immediately follows an opening one.
Technique and why it applies: A primitive pair at depth d contributes 2^(d-1); all such primitive pairs sum to the score by the recursive definition.
Invariant: level is the current nesting depth, and result is the contribution of all primitive pairs closed so far.
Edge cases: The code assumes the string is balanced. Empty input returns zero. The previous-character check only counts immediate () pairs, which is sufficient for the standard score rule.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Evaluate the score of a balanced parentheses string.
Idea: Use a stack of partial scores, pushing a fresh frame for each opening parenthesis.
Technique and why it applies: On closing a pair, its score is max(1, 2*last): an empty pair scores one, and a nested score doubles. The result is added to the enclosing frame.
Invariant: Each stack entry accumulates the score for the currently open parentheses level.
Edge cases: The code assumes balanced input and nonempty stack when processing a closing parenthesis. Empty input returns the initial score zero.
Complexity: Each parenthesis is pushed or popped once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string under the nested-doubling rule.
Idea: Track depth and add 2^depth for each primitive pair immediately closed.
Technique and why it applies: When a closing parenthesis follows an opening one, the pair contributes 2 raised to the number of enclosing levels. Depth is decremented before the contribution is added.
Invariant: depth is the number of currently open parentheses, and result accumulates all primitive-pair contributions.
Edge cases: The code assumes valid balanced parentheses. For a leading closing parenthesis, S[i-1] would wrap to the last character in Python, so invalid inputs are not safely handled.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Minimize the total wage paid to exactly k workers, where all hired workers must receive the same wage-to-quality ratio and at least their minimum wage.
Idea: Sort workers by wage/quality ratio and maintain the k smallest qualities in a max-heap among workers considered.
Technique and why it applies: At a chosen ratio, total pay is ratio times total quality. Keeping the smallest k qualities minimizes that cost for the current maximum ratio.
Invariant: pq stores negative qualities for the currently selected k workers, and kSmallest is their total quality.
Edge cases: heapq and heappop/heappush are used without imports in the snippet. The initial k workers are taken from the lowest ratios, and later candidates replace the largest quality if they improve the sum.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n) and heap updates are O(n log k), with O(n) storage for the sorted list and O(k) heap space.
